# AF 第九章 原文（重制基线）

## Chapter 9

[P01] Boxer's split（分裂） hoof（蹄） was slow to get better. They began to rebuild the windmill（风车） the next day. Boxer would not rest even one day. He hid his pain. In the evening he told Clover the hoof hurt. Clover put wet herbs（草药） on it. She and Benjamin told him to work less. "A horse's lungs（肺） do not last for ever," she said. But Boxer did not listen.

[P02] He said he had one wish left—to see the windmill working before he was too old to work. Long ago, the retiring（退休） age was set at twelve for horses and pigs, fourteen for cows, nine for dogs, seven for sheep, and five for hens and geese. They agreed on good pensions（养老金） for old animals. No animal had retired（退休的） yet, but they talked about it more and more. A small field was kept for barley（大麦）, and a corner of the pasture（牧场） would be fenced off as a grass field for old animals.

[P03] For a horse, the pension（养老金） would be five pounds of corn a day. In winter, fifteen pounds of hay（干草）. On holidays, a carrot or maybe an apple. Boxer would turn twelve next summer. Life was hard. The winter was as cold as the last one, and food was even less. All rations（配给） were cut again, except for the pigs and dogs. Squealer said strict equality（平等） in food would go against Animalism（动物主义）. He had no trouble proving they were not really short of food, no matter how it looked.

[P04] Now, they had to change the food a little (Squealer called it a "readjustment（调整）," never a "reduction（减少）"). But life was much better than in Jones's day. He read out the numbers fast and loud. They had more oats（燕麦）, more hay, more turnips（萝卜）. They worked shorter hours, drank better water, and lived longer. More of their young ones lived. They had more straw（稻草） and fewer fleas（跳蚤）.

[P05] The animals believed everything they heard. To tell the truth, Jones and all he stood for had almost gone from their memories. They knew life now was hard and plain. They were often hungry and cold. They worked when they were not sleeping. But surely the old days were worse. They were glad to think so. In those days they were slaves; now they were free. That was the great difference, as Squealer always said.

[P06] In autumn the four mother pigs had babies at the same time. They had thirty-one young pigs. The young pigs had two colours, and Napoleon was the only male（雄性） pig, so everyone knew their father. Later, a school would be built. For now, Napoleon taught the young pigs in the kitchen. They could not play with other young animals. Also, when a pig met another animal, the other animal had to step aside（旁边）. All pigs could wear green ribbons（丝带） on Sundays. The farm had a good year, but it had little money.

[P07] They needed to buy bricks（砖块）, sand, and lime（石灰） for the schoolroom（教室）, and save money for the windmill machines. They bought lamp oil, candles, sugar for Napoleon (other pigs could not have sugar because it made them fat), and other things like tools, nails（钉子）, string, coal, wire（电线）, old iron, and dog biscuits. They sold some hay and potatoes. They had to give six hundred eggs a week, so the hens could only hatch（孵化） enough chicks to keep the same number.

[P08] In December, the animals' food was cut, and in February it was cut again. Lanterns in the stalls（畜栏） were not allowed, to save oil. But the pigs looked fine, and even got fatter. One afternoon in late February, a warm, rich smell came from the little brew（酿造）-house beyond the kitchen. The animals sniffed（嗅） the air hungrily（饥饿地） and wondered if a warm mash（糊状饲料） was being made for their supper. But no warm mash came, and the next Sunday it was announced that all barley would be kept for the pigs.

[P09] The field past the orchard（果园） had already been planted with barley. Soon everyone knew that each pig now got a pint（品脱） of beer every day, and Napoleon himself got half a gallon（加仑）. It was always served to him in the Crown（王冠） Derby（德比） soup tureen（大碗）. Life was still hard, but it was better than before. There were more songs, more speeches, and more parades（游行）. Napoleon ordered a Spontaneous（自发的） Demonstration（示范） every week, to celebrate the struggles（斗争） and victories of Animal Farm.

[P10] At the right time the animals stopped work and walked around the farm in a line, like soldiers. The pigs went first, then the horses, cows, sheep, chickens and other birds. The dogs walked on both sides, and Napoleon's black cockerel（小公鸡） led them all. Boxer and Clover carried a green flag with a hoof and a horn. Then animals said poems, and Squealer spoke about more food. Sometimes a gun was fired.

[P11] The sheep were the biggest fans of the Spontaneous Demonstration. If anyone complained that the Spontaneous Demonstration wasted time and meant standing around in the cold, the sheep would stop him with a loud bleating of "Four legs good, two legs bad!"But most of the animals liked these celebrations（庆祝）. It made them feel good to remember that they were their own masters, and that their work was for their own good. So with the songs, the parades, Squealer's lists of numbers, the loud gun, the crowing（啼叫） of the cockerel, and the flag waving in the wind, they could forget their empty（空的） bellies（腹部）, at least for part of the time.

[P12] There was only one candidate（候选人）, Napoleon, and all the animals voted for him. That same day, they said new papers were found. These papers showed more about how Snowball helped Jones. Before, the animals thought Snowball only tried to lose the Battle of the Cowshed（牛棚） by a trick. But now it seemed he fought openly on Jones's side. In fact, he led the human soldiers and ran into battle shouting "Long live Humanity（人类）!" The wounds on Snowball's back were made by Napoleon's teeth.

[P13] He was the same. He did no work and always talked about Sugarcandy（糖块） Mountain. He sat on a stump（树桩）, moved his black wings, and talked for hours. "Up there, comrades（同志们）," he said, pointing to the sky with his big beak（鸟嘴）, "past that dark cloud—Sugarcandy Mountain is there, a happy place where we poor animals will rest from our work!" He said he had been there once and saw endless fields and sweet food.

[P14] Many animals believed him. They thought their lives were hungry and full of work. So it was right that a better world should be somewhere else. But it was hard to know what the pigs thought of Moses. They said his stories were lies, but they let him stay on the farm and do no work. They gave him a gill（鳃） of beer every day.

[P15] Sometimes the long hours and little food were hard, but Boxer never stopped trying. He never showed his strength was less. Only his coat was less shiny（闪亮） and his back legs seemed smaller. The others said, "Boxer will get better when the spring grass comes." But spring came, and Boxer did not get fatter. Sometimes on the hill, when he pushed a big rock, it seemed only his will kept him standing.

[P16] At these times his lips（嘴唇） moved and seemed to say, "I will work harder," but he had no voice left. Clover and Benjamin told him to rest, but Boxer did not listen. His twelfth birthday was near. He did not care what happened, if he piled up a good store of stone before he rested. Late one summer evening, a rumour（谣言） ran round the farm that something had happened to Boxer. He had gone alone to pull a load（负载） of stone. Two pigeons flew in fast with the news: "Boxer has fallen!"

[P17] He is lying（躺） on his side and can't（不能） get up!" Half the animals ran to the knoll（小丘）. Boxer lay between the cart's shafts（车辕）, his neck stretched（伸展） out, not able to lift his head. His eyes were dull（沉闷）, his sides wet with sweat（汗水）. Blood ran from his mouth. Clover went down on her knees by him. "Boxer!" she cried, "how are you?" "It is my lung（肺）," said Boxer weakly. "It does not matter. You can finish the windmill without me.

[P18] A lot of stone is saved up. I had one more month anyway. I was glad to rest. Benjamin is old too, so they may let him rest and stay with me." "We must get help now," said Clover. "Run and tell Squealer." The other animals ran back to the farmhouse（农舍）. Only Clover stayed. Only Clover remained, and Benjamin lay by Boxer's side and, without speaking, kept the flies off him with his long tail.

[P19] Soon Squealer came. He looked sad. He said Napoleon was sad about this bad luck. Boxer was one of the best workers, and Napoleon would send him to the hospital in Willingdon. The animals felt worried. No animal had ever left the farm before. They did not like to think of Boxer with humans. But Squealer made them believe the doctor in Willingdon could treat Boxer better.

[P20] About half an hour later, Boxer felt better. He got up slowly and limped（跛行） back to his stall（畜栏）. Clover and Benjamin made a bed of straw for him. For two days Boxer stayed there. The pigs sent pink medicine. Clover gave it to him twice a day. In the evenings she lay in his stall and talked to him, while Benjamin kept the flies off. Benjamin kept the flies off him. Boxer said he did not feel sorry for what had happened.

[P21] If he got better, he might live three more years. He wanted quiet days in a corner of the big field. It would be his first free time to learn and make his mind better. He wanted to learn the other twenty-two letters of the alphabet（字母表）. But Benjamin and Clover could only be with Boxer after work. The van（货车） came to take him away in the middle of the day. The animals were pulling turnips with a pig watching. Then they were surprised to see Benjamin running from the farm buildings, calling out loud.

[P22] For the first time, Benjamin was excited. For the first time, anyone saw him run. "Quick, quick!" he shouted. "Come now! They're taking Boxer away! Without waiting for the pig's orders, the animals stopped work and ran back. In the yard was a big closed van with two horses. A sly（狡猾的） man in a low hat sat on the driver's seat. Boxer's stall was empty. The animals stood round the van. "Good-bye, Boxer!" they said together, "good-bye!" "Fools! Fools!" shouted Benjamin, jumping round them and hitting the ground with his small hoofs（蹄）.

[P23] "Fools! Can you not read what is on that van?" The animals stopped and all was quiet. Muriel began to read. But Benjamin pushed her away and read in the silence: "Alfred Simmonds, Horse Slaughterer and Glue Boiler, Willingdon. Seller of Hides and Bone-Meal. Kennels（狗舍） Supplied." They are taking Boxer to the knacker（屠夫）'s（屠马场）!" The animals cried out in horror（恐怖）. Just then the man whipped his horses, and the van drove out of the yard at a quick trot（疾走）.

[P24] All the animals ran after it, crying loudly. Clover pushed to the front. The van went faster. She got to a slow run. "Boxer!" she cried. "Boxer! Boxer!" Boxer's face, with the white stripe（条纹） on his nose, came to the small window at the back. "Boxer!" cried Clover. "Get out! They are taking you to your death!" All the animals cried, "Get out, Boxer, get out!" But the van was going faster and moving away.

[P25] It was not clear if Boxer heard Clover. But soon his face went from the window, and they heard a loud drumming（击鼓） of hoofs（蹄） inside the van. He tried to kick his way out. Long ago, a few kicks from Boxer could break the van. But his strength was gone now. Soon the drumming grew softer and stopped. The animals called to the two horses that pulled the van. "Comrades, comrades!" they shouted. "Don't（不） take your brother to his death!" But the stupid animals did not understand. They just put back their ears and went faster.

[P26] Boxer did not come back at the window. Someone thought of shutting the gate too late, but the van was already through the 5-barred gate and going fast down the road. Boxer was never seen again. Three days later, the animals were told by Squealer that he had died in the hospital at Willingdon. Squealer said he had been there at the end. "It was the most moving thing I have ever seen!" Squealer said, and wiped away a tear with his trotter.

[P27] At the end, he was too weak to speak much. He whispered（低语） he was sad to die before the windmill was finished. 'Forward, comrades!' he whispered. 'Long live Animal Farm! Long live Comrade（同志） Napoleon! Napoleon is always right.' Those were his last words, comrades." Here Squealer's demeanour suddenly changed. Then Squealer changed. He was silent. His little eyes looked from side to side with doubt. Then he went on. He said a foolish and bad rumour had gone round when Boxer was taken away.

[P28] Some animals saw the van that took Boxer away had "Horse Slaughterer（屠夫）" on it. They thought Boxer was sent to the knacker's. Squealer said it was almost unbelievable（难以置信） that any animal could be so stupid. He cried, moving his tail, "Surely you know your beloved（心爱的） Leader, Comrade Napoleon, better than that?" But the explanation was very simple. The van was the knacker's before, and the veterinary（兽医的） surgeon（外科医生） bought it. He had not yet painted the old name out. That was how the mistake happened. The animals were very relieved（松了一口气） to hear this.

[P29] When Squealer told them more about Boxer's death, the good care he had, and the costly medicines Napoleon paid for, their last doubts went away. They were sad, but felt better knowing he died happy.

Napoleon came to the meeting the next Sunday morning and gave a short speech for Boxer. He said they could not bring back Boxer's body to bury on the farm, but he had ordered a big wreath（花圈） from the farmhouse garden sent to Boxer's grave（坟墓）.

[P30] In a few days, the pigs planned a big dinner to remember Boxer. Napoleon ended his speech by recalling Boxer's two favourite sayings（谚语）, "I will work harder" and "Comrade Napoleon is always right." He said every animal should make them his own. That night there was loud singing, then what sounded like a big quarrel（争吵）, and it ended at about eleven with a huge crash（碰撞） of glass. No one moved before noon the next day, and word went round that the pigs had bought another case of whisky（威士忌）.
